title: That Is An Award Winning Health Satire Publication to You
subtitle: The Frontier Psychiatrists newsletter wins a SWAAY award for best blog in healthcare
body_html:
Healthcare marketing is hard. It’s regulated to a level that would make airlines shiver. For example, in the State of New York, patient testimonials—a mainstay of marketing in any other field of endeavor—are not just forbidden but illegal, if they lack specific, verifiable data.

So, it’s hard. We need to tell humans hope for their health problems exist! And, at the same time, we have to comply with complex regulations and ethical standards to uphold for the protection of the vulnerable.

One organization that helps support marketing professionals is SWAAY, and I was thrilled to be nominated for their blog of the year award. Spoiler alert, I won.

So now, when anyone asks you what you're doing with your phone, you can just tell them you're reading an award-winning blog.

It's still not a good excuse for what you're doing on your phone all the time. Put it down, it'll be here later.

I will wait.

A few comments on marketing in healthcare:

People treat marketing like it's not a necessity. We spent a lot of time creating products, treatments, service lines, and some of those products are great, and could help a lot of people.

But, at least in healthcare, people might not know about them. Marketing is getting out the word. It's letting people know something exists in a way that's compelling, useful, and effective. The number of people who will get to remission from a magical perfect treatment who never hear about it? It is still zero.

This is not unimportant work. There is a lot of functionally anti-healthcare marketing out there, things like anti-care propaganda, that starts as “just asking questions,” and always seems to end in one grift or another. That's marketing too. Dubious supplements are a product that bypasses all of the rigor, evidence, and is all about the marketing. They're able to start their marketing differently from regulated healthcare products, with effective scaremongering and robust lies. Using statements designed to kick the fear center of the brain into action, you are more likely to believe whatever marketing message comes next, and inspire you to buy whatever their “wellness product” may be. There are people who choose to do that kind of work, and they make a lot of money doing it.

People who chose healthcare marketing are making the opposite choice. They are deciding to work in a complex and difficult system, with a lot of barriers to protect us from lies about things that actually could harm us, and that's valiant. It's important. It lets people know there's hope. That's why strategists like Shereese Maynard (standing with me in Coronado today!) are so important. Without their work, we wouldn't know Hope is out there, and the systems that are necessary to make that possible wouldn't exist.

Not all healthcare marketing is benign— obviously. That's why it's so heavily regulated. Not all regulation solves all problems. But if it wasn't for marketing efforts for healthcare products, we wouldn't know they exist, except maybe by word-of-mouth. And the problems we have as humans? We deserve to know they have solutions, if they exist. Most people don't have to think about a healthcare problem until they're experiencing it, or someone that love is experiencing it. People aren't lusting after depression treatments like they are designer bags, until they're depressed, and then they literally rather die than continue to put up with it some of the time.

I want to thank people who do healthcare marketing. I also want to encourage all of us to spread the word, when we have a great healing experience, to tell people in your life about it. Let people know that hope exists, and that you were treated decently, when that's the thing that happens. Spread the word when there's something great.

The Frontier Psychiatrists is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
